questions.stem: What is the vapour pressure of a liquid?
options: The pressure of the air above the liquid in an open container at sea level
The pressure the liquid exerts on the bottom of the container that holds it
The pressure of its vapour in equilibrium with the liquid in a closed container
The pressure needed to turn all of the liquid into a gas at room temperature
questions.explanation: In a closed container molecules escape the liquid and return to it until the rates are equal; the pressure of the vapour then is the vapour pressure. It depends on the substance and the temperature.

questions.stem: Diethyl ether has a much higher vapour pressure than water at 25 degrees C. What does this indicate?
options: The covalent bonds in diethyl ether are weaker than those in water
Diethyl ether molecules are lighter than water molecules, so they escape
Water molecules move faster than diethyl ether molecules at 25 degrees C
The intermolecular forces in diethyl ether are weaker than those in water
questions.explanation: Molecules escape the liquid more easily when the forces between molecules are weak, giving a high vapour pressure. Water's hydrogen bonding holds its molecules together strongly. Evaporation does not break covalent bonds within molecules.

questions.stem: How does the vapour pressure of a liquid change as it is heated, and when does it boil?
options: Vapour pressure stays constant; it boils when the liquid reaches 100 degrees C
Vapour pressure rises; it boils when vapour pressure equals the external pressure
Vapour pressure falls; it boils when vapour pressure drops to zero
Vapour pressure rises; it boils when vapour pressure is twice the external pressure
questions.explanation: Heating gives more molecules enough energy to escape, so vapour pressure rises. Boiling occurs when bubbles of vapour can form inside the liquid, which happens when vapour pressure equals the surrounding pressure.

questions.stem: On a high mountain, water boils at about 85 degrees C. Why?
options: Gravity is weaker, so the water molecules escape from the liquid more easily
Air pressure is lower, so vapour pressure matches it at a lower temperature
Air is colder, so water molecules need less energy to break their covalent bonds
There is less oxygen, so the hydrogen bonds between water molecules are weaker
questions.explanation: Boiling point is the temperature at which vapour pressure equals external pressure. With less air pressure above it, water reaches that point at a lower temperature. The hydrogen bonds themselves are unchanged.

questions.stem: The boiling points of the alkanes rise from methane (CH₄) to butane (C₄H₁₀). What is the best explanation?
options: Larger molecules form more hydrogen bonds, because they contain more hydrogen
Larger molecules are more polar, so their dipole-dipole forces are stronger
Larger molecules have stronger C-H covalent bonds, which are broken on boiling
Larger molecules have more electrons, so their dispersion forces are stronger
questions.explanation: Alkanes are non-polar, so only dispersion forces act between their molecules, and these grow with the number of electrons and the surface area of contact. Alkanes cannot hydrogen bond, and boiling does not break covalent bonds.

questions.stem: Pentane (a straight chain) boils at 36 degrees C, while its isomer 2,2-dimethylpropane (a compact, nearly spherical molecule) boils at 10 degrees C. Why?
options: The branched molecules are polar, so they repel each other and boil more easily
The branched molecules form hydrogen bonds, which are weaker than dispersion forces
Straight chains have more surface contact, so dispersion forces are stronger
The straight chains contain more electrons, so their dispersion forces are stronger
questions.explanation: Both have the formula C₅H₁₂ and the same number of electrons, so the difference comes from shape: long chains can lie alongside each other, giving more contact and stronger dispersion forces than compact spheres.

questions.stem: Ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) and dimethyl ether (CH₃OCH₃) have the same formula, C₂H₆O. Ethanol boils at 78 degrees C and dimethyl ether at -24 degrees C. Why?
options: Ethanol has an O-H group, so its molecules hydrogen bond to each other
Ethanol has more electrons, so its dispersion forces are much stronger
Dimethyl ether has an O-H group, which weakens its intermolecular forces
Dimethyl ether is ionic, so its particles separate easily when heated
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding needs a hydrogen atom bonded directly to N, O or F. Ethanol has an O-H group; in dimethyl ether every hydrogen is bonded to carbon, so only weaker dipole-dipole and dispersion forces act. The two have the same number of electrons.

questions.stem: Fluorine and chlorine are gases at room temperature, bromine is a liquid and iodine is a solid. Which explanation is correct?
options: Hydrogen bonding becomes stronger as the halogen atoms become larger down the group
The covalent bond within each molecule becomes stronger going down the group
The molecules become more polar going down the group, so dipole forces increase
Dispersion forces strengthen as the number of electrons increases
questions.explanation: The halogens are non-polar diatomic molecules held together only by dispersion forces, which strengthen with more electrons. The covalent bonds within the molecules actually become weaker down the group.

questions.stem: Four substances of small molar mass are compared. Which would you expect to boil at the highest temperature?
options: Neon, Ne
Water, H₂O
Hydrogen sulfide, H₂S
Methane, CH₄
questions.explanation: Water molecules form strong hydrogen bonds with each other, so water boils at 100 degrees C. Hydrogen sulfide, though larger, has only dipole-dipole and dispersion forces and is a gas at room temperature.

questions.stem: A student shakes ethanol with water and hexane with water. The ethanol mixes completely but the hexane forms a separate layer. What explains this?
options: Ethanol can hydrogen bond with water molecules; hexane cannot
Ethanol is ionic and separates into ions; hexane is covalent
Hexane is denser than water, so it sinks and cannot mix
Hexane reacts with water to form a separate layer of product
questions.explanation: A substance dissolves when the attractions it can form with the solvent are similar in strength to those it replaces. Ethanol's O-H group hydrogen bonds with water; non-polar hexane would disrupt water's hydrogen bonds without replacing them. Hexane is less dense than water and floats.

questions.stem: The solubility of alcohols in water decreases from methanol to hexan-1-ol. What is the best explanation?
options: Longer alcohols react with water, which removes them from the solution
The longer non-polar chain disrupts hydrogen bonding with water more and more
The O-H group becomes less polar as the chain gets longer, so it bonds less
Longer alcohols have fewer electrons, so they form weaker forces with water
questions.explanation: Every alcohol has one O-H group that can hydrogen bond with water, but the growing hydrocarbon chain is non-polar and cannot. As the chain lengthens, the non-polar part dominates and solubility falls.

questions.stem: Iodine (I₂) dissolves well in hexane but only slightly in water. Which statement explains this?
options: Iodine is ionic, and ionic substances dissolve only in non-polar solvents like hexane
Hexane is denser than water, so it holds more iodine molecules per litre
Iodine and hexane are both non-polar, so they attract by similar dispersion forces
Iodine forms hydrogen bonds with hexane but cannot form hydrogen bonds with water
questions.explanation: Like dissolves like: non-polar iodine and hexane interact by dispersion forces, so mixing them costs little energy. To dissolve in water, iodine would have to break water's strong hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide (linear) and sulfur dioxide (bent) both contain polar bonds. Sulfur dioxide boils at -10 degrees C, but carbon dioxide turns to gas at -78 degrees C. Why the difference?
options: CO₂ has stronger covalent bonds, which must be broken before it can boil
SO₂ is a polar molecule with dipole-dipole forces; CO₂'s bond dipoles cancel
CO₂ is a polar molecule with dipole-dipole forces; SO₂'s bond dipoles cancel
SO₂ forms hydrogen bonds between its molecules; CO₂ forms dispersion forces
questions.explanation: In linear CO₂ the two C=O dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, so the molecule is non-polar. Bent SO₂ has a net dipole, adding dipole-dipole forces to its dispersion forces. Neither can hydrogen bond.

questions.stem: Using molecular shape and bond polarity, which of these molecules has an overall dipole?
options: Carbon dioxide, CO₂
Ammonia, NH₃
Methane, CH₄
Carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄
questions.explanation: Ammonia is trigonal pyramidal, with a lone pair on nitrogen, so its N-H bond dipoles do not cancel. The other molecules are symmetrical (tetrahedral or linear), so their bond dipoles cancel.

questions.stem: In chromatography, what causes the components of a mixture to separate?
options: Differences in their colours, which make them absorb light from the solvent
Differences in their boiling points, which make some components evaporate
Differences in their masses, which make heavier components sink faster
How strongly each is attracted to the stationary and mobile phases
questions.explanation: Each component is shared between the stationary and mobile phases. A component attracted more strongly to the stationary phase moves more slowly, so the components spread out.

questions.stem: On a TLC plate, the solvent front moved 9.0 cm from the baseline and a spot moved 3.6 cm. What is the Rf value of the spot?
questions.explanation: Rf = distance moved by the spot / distance moved by the solvent front = 3.6 / 9.0 = 0.40. Dividing the other way gives 2.5; an Rf value is never greater than 1.

questions.stem: A TLC plate uses polar silica as the stationary phase and a non-polar solvent. Which component would have the lowest Rf value?
options: The most volatile component
The component used in excess
The most polar component
The least polar component
questions.explanation: A polar component is strongly attracted to the polar silica and only weakly carried by the non-polar solvent, so it moves least. Non-polar components travel near the solvent front.

questions.stem: Why is the baseline on a TLC plate drawn in pencil and placed above the level of the solvent?
options: Pencil does not dissolve and run, and the spots must not dissolve into the solvent pool
Pencil absorbs the solvent faster, and the spots must start below the solvent surface
Pencil marks glow under UV light, and the solvent must cover the spots to dissolve them
Pencil is polar, and placing it above the solvent keeps the plate from drying out
questions.explanation: Ink would separate and move with the solvent, confusing the results. If the spots were below the solvent surface they would wash off into the solvent instead of travelling up the plate.

questions.stem: A food dye gives three spots on TLC. Standard dyes A, B and C, run on the same plate, give Rf values of 0.25, 0.55 and 0.70; the food dye's spots have Rf values 0.25, 0.48 and 0.70. What can be concluded?
options: It contains dyes A and C, plus one dye that is not B
It contains dyes A, B and C and no other component
It contains dye B only, which has separated into three spots
It is a pure substance, since three spots form on the plate
questions.explanation: Spots that match standards on the same plate under the same conditions suggest A and C are present. The spot at 0.48 does not match B (0.55), so it is a different substance. A pure substance gives one spot.

questions.stem: How does TLC show whether a synthesised compound is pure?
options: A pure compound gives no spots, because it does not move
A pure compound gives a spot exactly at the solvent front
A pure compound gives one spot for each element it contains
A pure compound gives a single spot that matches the standard
questions.explanation: Impurities usually have different attractions to the two phases and appear as extra spots. One spot matching a pure standard, run under the same conditions, indicates purity.

questions.stem: Which substance acts as the mobile phase when a sample is analysed by gas chromatography (GC)?
options: An unreactive carrier gas, such as helium or nitrogen
A liquid solvent pumped through the column at high pressure
A thin layer of silica coated on a sheet of glass or plastic
A high-boiling liquid coated on the inside of the column
questions.explanation: GC carries vaporised samples through a column with an unreactive gas. The high-boiling liquid coating the column is the stationary phase, and a liquid pumped at high pressure is the mobile phase in HPLC.

questions.stem: In GC, what is the retention time of a component?
options: The time the detector takes to measure the area under the peak
The time from injection until that component reaches the detector
The time a component takes to be vaporised in the heated injection port
The time the carrier gas takes to travel through an empty column
questions.explanation: Retention time depends on how strongly a component interacts with the stationary phase. Under identical conditions a substance always has the same retention time, so comparing with standards identifies components.

questions.stem: A GC chromatogram of a fuel shows peaks with areas of 30 and 90 units for two components only. Assuming the detector responds equally to both, what percentage of the mixture is the second component?
questions.explanation: Peak area is proportional to the amount of a component: 90 / (30 + 90) x 100 = 75%. 25% is the first component, and 33% compares the peaks with each other rather than with the total.

questions.stem: Why is HPLC rather than GC used to analyse substances such as sugars and many drugs?
options: They are too volatile for HPLC, so they must be analysed as gases in a GC column instead
HPLC separates substances by mass, while GC can separate only substances of equal mass
HPLC uses a gas mobile phase, which carries large molecules better than a liquid does
They decompose before vaporising, and HPLC needs no vaporisation of the sample
questions.explanation: GC requires the sample to be vaporised, which destroys many large or heat-sensitive molecules. HPLC pushes a liquid mobile phase through a tightly packed column at high pressure, so no vaporisation is needed.

questions.stem: In an HPLC column with a non-polar stationary phase and a polar mobile phase, which component of a mixture elutes first?
options: The least polar component, as it is carried well by the mobile phase
The most polar component, as it is held strongly by the stationary phase
The largest molecule, as large molecules always travel fastest in HPLC
The most polar component, as it is carried well by the mobile phase
questions.explanation: A polar component prefers the polar mobile phase and interacts weakly with the non-polar stationary phase, so it has the shortest retention time. Non-polar components are held back.

questions.stem: An athlete's urine is tested for a banned drug by HPLC. How is the drug identified?
options: The drug changes the retention times of every other peak in the sample
A peak appears at the same retention time as a standard sample of the drug
The largest peak in the chromatogram is always the drug being tested for
The drug produces a peak with a colour that matches a printed colour chart
questions.explanation: Run under identical conditions, the drug has a characteristic retention time, so a matching peak suggests its presence; the peak area against standards gives the amount. Confirmation usually uses a second technique.

questions.stem: According to kinetic theory, what causes the pressure of a gas in a container?
options: Gas particles colliding with the walls of the container
Gas particles attracting each other strongly in the middle
Gas particles being pulled downward by gravity onto the base
Gas particles expanding in size until they fill the container
questions.explanation: Particles in constant random motion strike the walls and exert a force on them; pressure is that force per unit area. Particles themselves do not expand, and attractions between gas particles are very weak.

questions.stem: Which statement is part of the kinetic theory model of a gas?
options: The particles are stationary until heated, and then start to move in one direction
The particles lose energy at every collision, so the gas slowly cools and settles
The particles' average kinetic energy is proportional to the kelvin temperature
The particles take up most of the volume of the container, leaving little space
questions.explanation: Kinetic theory treats gas particles as tiny, widely spaced and in rapid random motion, with elastic collisions and an average kinetic energy proportional to absolute temperature. Losing energy at collisions would make pressure fall over time.

questions.stem: A sealed syringe of air is pushed in to half its volume at constant temperature. What happens to the pressure, and why?
options: It stays the same, because the number of particles has not changed
It increases, because particles hit each unit area of wall more often
It decreases, because particles have less room to build up their speed
It increases, because each particle moves faster when it is squeezed
questions.explanation: With the same particles in a smaller space, collisions with the walls are more frequent, so pressure rises (it roughly doubles). At constant temperature the particles' average speed does not change.

questions.stem: A bicycle tyre pumped up in the cool morning feels harder in the afternoon sun. Why?
options: Warmer gas particles become larger, so they take up more of the tyre
Sunlight adds extra gas particles to the tyre through the rubber walls
Warmer gas particles attract each other more, pulling on the tyre walls
Warmer gas particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often
questions.explanation: At almost constant volume, a higher temperature raises the particles' average kinetic energy, so they collide with the walls more often and with more force, increasing pressure.

questions.stem: A balloon is moved from a warm room into a freezer, at constant pressure. What happens, and why?
options: It shrinks, because some gas particles are destroyed at low temperature
It stays the same size, because the number of gas particles is unchanged
It shrinks, because slower particles need less volume for the same pressure
It expands, because cold air is denser and pushes outwards on the rubber
questions.explanation: Cooling lowers the particles' average speed, so they strike the walls less often and less hard. To keep the pressure equal to the air outside, the volume decreases until collisions per unit area are restored.

questions.stem: Why do warnings on aerosol cans say not to heat them or throw them into a fire?
options: Heating makes the gas particles combine into larger particles that block the valve
At fixed volume, the gas pressure rises with temperature until the can may burst
At fixed volume, the gas pressure falls with temperature until the can collapses
Heating changes the gas into a liquid, which expands and splits the metal can
questions.explanation: The can is rigid, so its volume is fixed. Heating increases the speed of the gas particles and the force and frequency of their collisions, so pressure rises and can exceed what the can withstands.

questions.stem: At the same temperature, ammonia (M = 17 g/mol) diffuses along a tube faster than hydrogen chloride (M = 36.5 g/mol). Why?
options: Ammonia molecules have more kinetic energy than hydrogen chloride molecules at the same temperature
Hydrogen chloride molecules attract the air in the tube, which stops them moving
Ammonia is a liquid at room temperature, so it flows faster than hydrogen chloride gas
At equal temperature both have the same average kinetic energy, so the lighter molecules move faster
questions.explanation: Equal temperature means equal average kinetic energy, and since kinetic energy depends on mass and speed, lighter particles must move faster on average. Both are gases at room temperature.

questions.stem: At 20 °C the vapour pressures of three liquids are: propanone 24 kPa, ethanol 5.9 kPa and water 2.3 kPa. Which statement is correct?
options: Propanone boils at the highest temperature; ethanol has the strongest intermolecular forces
All three boil at the same temperature, because the vapour pressures are all below 101 kPa
Propanone boils at the lowest temperature; water has the strongest intermolecular forces
Water boils at the lowest temperature; propanone has the strongest intermolecular forces
questions.explanation: Weak intermolecular forces let molecules escape easily, giving a high vapour pressure, so propanone reaches atmospheric pressure at the lowest temperature. Water's low vapour pressure reflects its extensive hydrogen bonding.

questions.stem: More air is pumped into a basketball, whose volume stays about the same, at constant temperature. According to kinetic theory, why does the pressure rise?
options: More particles hit each unit area of the wall every second
Each particle moves faster, so it hits the wall much harder
The particles grow larger as they are squeezed into the ball
The particles attract each other more strongly when crowded
questions.explanation: At constant temperature the particles' average speed is unchanged, but adding more particles to the same volume increases how often they collide with the walls. The size of the particles does not change.

questions.stem: According to kinetic theory, what happens to the particles of a gas as it is cooled at constant volume?
options: Their attractions to each other disappear, so they move further apart
Their average kinetic energy falls, so they hit the walls less often and less hard
Their size decreases, so they take up less of the container and the pressure falls
Their number decreases, because some particles stop moving and leave the gas
questions.explanation: Temperature is a measure of the particles' average kinetic energy. Slower particles strike the walls less frequently and with less force, so the pressure falls. The particles themselves do not shrink.

questions.stem: In paper chromatography of a black ink with water as the solvent, one coloured spot stays on the baseline. What does this show?
options: That component is insoluble in water, so it stays attracted to the paper
That component is very soluble in water, so it travels with the solvent
That component has an Rf value of 1, because it did not move at all
That component is the solvent, so it cannot be separated from the ink
questions.explanation: A substance moves only if it dissolves in the mobile phase. A spot that remains on the baseline has an Rf of 0; trying a less polar solvent may make it move.
